newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak money market liquidity crunch seen lasting.
newsitem.headline: Slovak money market liquidity crunch seen lasting.

text.p: The Slovak money market on Monday continued to suffer from a severe liquidity crunch, and analysts said they expect no significant liquidity to flow into the market in the near future.

The National Bank of Slovakia on Monday remained vigiliant in its strategy of keeping the local money market short of crowns while at the same time supporting the currency through a stronger-than-market official fix.
The NBS fight for the stability of the crown, which has been under pressure for over two weeks, has put a stranglehold on the market, but appears to have stopped speculative crown short selling.

"The central bank seems to be thinking that the pressure on the crown is still not over and it appears that they will not add too much liquidity to the market this week," said Martin Hrozany of Credit Lyonnais Bank.
As of June 2, the banking sector lacked around 15 billion crowns, or some 34.71 percent of the funds needed to meet its minimum reserve requirements later this month.

Hrozany said the crown's trend was likely to be further influenced by the movement of the Czech crown and that the Slovak currency was likely to ease once the NBS decides to replenish banks' crown positions.
"The crown looks stable at levels close to the NBS official rate, but it is an artificial situation since there is virtually no normal trading on the market due to low liquidity," he said.
The crown on Monday was trading at around -0.90 percent on the depreciation side of its mark/dollar basket parity in late afternoon activity.

The central bank fixed the crown at 33.454 to the dollar and at 19.483 to the mark, with a deviation against the basket of -0.67 percent. The crown was trading at around -1.087 versus the basket shortly before the fixing.
Hrozany said that the Slovak crown was likely to weaken by some three to four percent to find its real market value.
"It won't be a devaluation, the crown should not go beyond five percent in its weak side, but the weakening trend now seems natural given the trade deficit problems," he said.

Rasto Zivor of ING Bank said he expected the stalemate with low liquidity on the money market and the FX spot to continue for some time, but he warned that the liquidity crunch could soon become dangerous for banks' client relations.
"You cannot find any offers (for crowns) on the market at the moment and some local banks were willing even to pay 80 percent for crown deposits to improve liquidity," Zivor said.
Earlier on Monday, the NBS added 1.5 billion crowns through a one-day repo tender at 30 percent.
However, another Bratislava-based money market trader said the NBS would probably help improve liquidity at some banks if they get into more serious problems.

"The central bank may help those banks who were loyal to the Slovak currency and had limited their trade with foreign speculators a few days ago if these banks get to serious liquidity problems," the trader said.
"They can do it through individual repo tenders for example, as they already did once this year," he added.
